questions.question: What is the correct dimensional formula for surface tension?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**MT⁻²**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Surface tension** is defined as the force per unit length acting along the surface of a liquid, perpendicular to any line drawn on the surface.
 
• The formula for surface tension is given as **Force/Length**, where force is measured in **Newtons (N)** and length in **meters (m)**.
 
• In terms of dimensional analysis: **[Surface Tension] = [Force] × [Length^(-1)]**.
 
• The dimensional formula for force is **[M][L][T^(-2)]**. When divided by length **[L]**, the dimensional formula becomes **[M][T^(-2)]**.
 
• Hence, the correct dimensional formula for surface tension is **MT^(-2)**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Definition of Surface Tension:**

 
 
• Surface tension is a property of the liquid surface that arises due to the cohesive forces between liquid molecules.
 
• It enables a liquid to resist an external force, as seen in phenomena like water droplets forming spherical shapes or insects walking on water.
 
 
 
• **Units of Surface Tension:**
 
 
• The SI unit is **Newton per meter (N/m)**.
 
• In CGS, the unit is **dyne per centimeter**, where 1 N/m = 1000 dyne/cm.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Surface Tension:**
 
 
• Used in detergents and soaps to lower the surface tension of water, improving its cleaning action.
 
• Essential in biological processes like the movement of water in plants through capillary action.
 
• Helps in the design of medical devices like syringes and micropipettes.
 
 
 
• **Factors Affecting Surface Tension:**
 
 
• **Temperature:** Surface tension decreases with an increase in temperature.
 
• **Impurities:** The presence of soluble impurities can either increase or decrease surface tension depending on their nature.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Surface Energy:**

 
 
• Surface tension is directly related to surface energy, which is the energy required to increase the surface area of a liquid by a unit amount.
 
• Its dimensional formula is also **[M][T^(-2)]**, the same as surface tension.
 
 
 
• **Experimental Methods:**
 
 
• Surface tension is commonly measured using methods like the capillary rise method, drop weight method, or ring method (Du Noüy ring method).

questions.question: _______ is the SI unit used for measuring thermodynamic temperature.
questions.solution:
**The correct answer is 'Kelvin'**

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Kelvin (K):**

 
 
• The Kelvin is the base unit of temperature in the International System of Units (SI), having the unit symbol K.
 
• It is used to measure **thermodynamic temperature**, which is an absolute scale where zero (0 K) represents absolute zero—the point at which all thermal motion of particles ceases.
 
• Unlike the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales, the Kelvin scale does not use "degrees" (°); it is simply referred to as Kelvin.
 
• The Kelvin scale is widely used in physical sciences and engineering because it provides a direct measurement of the energy content of a system.
 
• The relation between Kelvin and Celsius is defined by the formula: **K = °C + 273.15**.
 
 

**Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Celsius (°C):**

 
 
• The Celsius scale is a derived unit of temperature in the SI system, primarily used for everyday weather and liquid measurements.
 
• It is based on the freezing point of water at 0°C and the boiling point at 100°C under standard atmospheric pressure.
 
• While it is widely used globally, it is not the standard SI unit for thermodynamic temperature.
 
 
 
• **Fahrenheit (°F):**
 
 
• The Fahrenheit scale is a temperature scale primarily used in the United States and some Caribbean countries.
 
• On this scale, the freezing point of water is 32°F and the boiling point is 212°F.
 
• It is not part of the SI system and is rarely used in scientific research.
 
 
 
• **Rankine (°R):**
 
 
• The Rankine scale is an absolute temperature scale that uses Fahrenheit degrees.
 
• Zero on the Rankine scale is absolute zero, but a Rankine degree is equal to one Fahrenheit degree.
 
• It is primarily used in certain engineering systems in the United States, but it is not an SI unit.
 
 

**Important Points__**

 
• The Kelvin was originally defined based on the **triple point of water** (273.16 K), which is the temperature at which water exists simultaneously as a solid, liquid, and gas.
 
• In **2019**, the definition of the Kelvin was updated to be based on the **Boltzmann constant (k)**, which relates thermal energy to temperature.
 
• This change ensures that the unit is defined by a fundamental physical constant rather than an experimental measurement of a specific substance.
 
• The lowest possible temperature is 0 K, and there are no negative values on the Kelvin scale.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct with respect to dimensional analysis?

options.text: An equation that is dimensionally consistent is always physically correct.
Dimensional analysis can verify both the magnitude and the physical validity of an equation.
Trigonometric and logarithmic functions are valid only when applied to quantities that are dimensionless.
Refractive index has dimensions because it involves the speed of light.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Trigonometric and logarithmic functions are valid only when applied to quantities that are dimensionless.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Trigonometric, logarithmic, and exponential functions** are mathematical operations that must take **dimensionless arguments**. For example, in the expression sin(theta) , the angle theta must be dimensionless. Similarly, in log(x) or e^x , x must be a pure number.
 
• An equation that is **dimensionally consistent** is not necessarily **physically correct**. For instance, the equation s = ut + at² is dimensionally consistent (all terms have dimensions of length), but it is physically incorrect because the correct kinematic formula is s = ut + (1)/(2)at² .
 
• **Dimensional analysis** cannot verify the **magnitude** or **dimensionless constants** in an equation. It only checks if the units on both sides of the equation are compatible.
 
• The **Refractive Index** is defined as the ratio of the speed of light in a vacuum to the speed of light in a medium ( n = c/v ). Since it is a ratio of two similar physical quantities (speeds), it is a **dimensionless quantity**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The **Principle of Homogeneity of Dimensions** states that the dimensions of all the terms in a physical expression must be the same.
 
• Other common **dimensionless quantities** include **strain**, **relative density**, **solid angle**, and **plane angle**.
 
• While dimensional analysis is a powerful tool for checking the consistency of equations and deriving relations, its main limitation is its inability to determine **proportionality constants** or handle **summation/difference** of terms that are not of the same dimension.

questions.question: Which of the following physical quantities is dimensionless?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Strain**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Strain** is a **dimensionless quantity** that represents the relative deformation or change in shape/size of a material under applied stress.
 
• It is defined as the ratio of change in length to the original length (*strain = ΔL / L*), where both ΔL and L have the same unit, making strain dimensionless.
 
• While **stress** and **pressure** involve force per unit area and have dimensions of force divided by area, strain only involves a ratio of lengths, and hence does not carry any physical dimensions.
 
• **Area** is a two-dimensional quantity with dimensions *L²*, and cannot be dimensionless.
 
• Since strain does not involve units or dimensions, it can be used universally across different systems for comparing relative deformation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Stress**:

 
 
• Stress is defined as the internal force per unit area exerted by a material when subjected to external forces.
 
• Its formula is *stress = Force / Area*, and its dimensional formula is **[M¹ L⁻¹ T⁻²]**.
 
• Stress is measured in units such as **Pascals (Pa)** or **Newton/m²**.
 
• Examples include tensile stress, compressive stress, and shear stress.
 
 
 
• **Pressure**:
 
 
• Pressure is the force exerted per unit area in a direction perpendicular to the surface.
 
• Its dimensional formula is **[M¹ L⁻¹ T⁻²]**, similar to stress.
 
• Pressure is measured in units such as **Pascals (Pa)**, **bar**, or **atmosphere**.
 
• Applications include fluid mechanics, meteorology, and engineering systems.
 
 
 
• **Area**:
 
 
• Area refers to the extent of a two-dimensional surface and is calculated as *length × breadth*.
 
• Its dimensional formula is **[L²]**.
 
• Units of area include **square meters (m²)**, **square centimeters (cm²)**, and **hectares**.
 
• Common uses include land measurement and geometric calculations.
 
 
 
• **Strain**:
 
 
• Strain represents the ratio of deformation to the original dimension and does not involve units or dimensions.
 
• Types of strain include **tensile strain**, **compressive strain**, and **shear strain**.
 
• Strain is crucial in material science and engineering for understanding how materials behave under stress.
 
• Examples include elongation in a wire or deformation in a beam under load.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Dimensionless quantities** are crucial in physics and engineering as they allow comparison across different systems without being restricted by units.
 
• Examples of dimensionless quantities include **strain**, **refractive index**, **Poisson’s ratio**, and **specific gravity**.
 
• Dimensionless quantities often represent ratios or pure numbers derived from physical quantities.
 
• They are widely used in scaling laws, similarity analysis, and mathematical modeling.

questions.question: What is the unit of energy in the MKS system of measurement?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Joule**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Joule** is the unit of energy in the **MKS system** (Meter-Kilogram-Second system) of measurement.
 
• It is defined as the **energy transferred** when a force of one Newton moves an object by one meter in the direction of the force.
 
• The formula for energy in Joules is expressed as **1 Joule = 1 Newton × 1 meter**.
 
• **James Prescott Joule**, a physicist, established the relationship between mechanical work and heat, leading to the naming of this unit after him.
 
• In the MKS system, the Joule is a derived unit, where 1 Joule corresponds to **1 kg·m²/s²** (kilogram meter squared per second squared).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Erg:**

 
 
• Erg is the unit of energy in the **CGS system** (Centimeter-Gram-Second system).
 
• It is much smaller than the Joule, where **1 Joule = 10⁷ Ergs**.
 
• It is defined as the energy transferred when a force of 1 dyne moves an object by 1 centimeter.
 
 
 
• **Volt:**
 
 
• Volt is the unit of **electric potential difference** or electromotive force.
 
• It is defined as the potential difference across a conductor when 1 ampere of current dissipates 1 watt of power.
 
• Volt is not a unit of energy but is related to energy in the context of electrical systems, such as in the calculation of work done by charges.
 
 
 
• **Mole:**
 
 
• Mole is the **unit of substance amount** in the SI system.
 
• It represents the quantity of a substance that contains as many elementary entities (atoms, molecules, ions, etc.) as there are atoms in 12 grams of carbon-12.
 
• While it is a fundamental unit in chemistry, it is not related to energy measurement.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Joule:**
 
 
• Used in physics and engineering to measure **mechanical work, heat energy, and electrical energy**.
 
• Examples include calculating the energy required to lift objects, the heat produced in a resistor, and the work done by machines.
 
• It is used in everyday appliances like light bulbs, where energy consumption is often expressed in **kilowatt-hours (kWh)**, which can be converted to Joules.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **James Prescott Joule:**

 
 
• Born in **1818**, he was an English physicist best known for his work on the relationship between heat and mechanical work.
 
• He formulated the law of conservation of energy, leading to the **first law of thermodynamics**.
 
• The unit "Joule" was named in his honor in recognition of his contributions to energy studies.
 
 
 
• **Energy Units in Different Systems:**
 
 
• The **MKS system** uses Joule as the standard unit of energy.
 
• The **CGS system** uses Erg, which is smaller than Joule.
 
• In the SI system, Joule is widely adopted as the universal unit for energy.
 
 
 
• **Conversion of Joules:**
 
 
• 1 Joule = **0.239 Calories** (used in food energy measurement).
 
• 1 Joule = **10⁷ Ergs** (used in smaller-scale physics applications).
 
• 1 Joule = **0.00027778 watt-hour** (used in electrical energy billing).

questions.question: The physical quantity that has both magnitude and direction is known as-
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Vectors**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Vectors** are physical quantities that have both **magnitude** and **direction**. Examples include velocity, acceleration, force, and displacement.
 
• A vector is typically represented graphically by an arrow. The length of the arrow indicates its magnitude, and the direction of the arrow represents its direction.
 
• Vectors are added or subtracted using the **triangle law** or **parallelogram law of vector addition**. This allows for the combination of magnitudes and directions in a structured way.
 
• The mathematical representation of a vector often includes components along coordinate axes, such as x, y, and z in a 3D space.
 
• Vectors are fundamental in describing various phenomena in **physics and engineering**, such as motion, forces, and fields.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Scalars:**

 
 
• Scalars are physical quantities that have **only magnitude** and no direction. Examples include mass, temperature, time, and energy.
 
• Unlike vectors, scalars can be added or subtracted directly without considering direction.
 
• Scalars are used in everyday measurements and calculations, such as determining distances or measuring temperature.
 
 
 
• **Vector Operations:**
 
 
• **Dot Product:** The dot product of two vectors is a scalar and is given by the formula A·B = |A||B|cos(θ), where θ is the angle between the vectors.
 
• **Cross Product:** The cross product of two vectors is a vector and is given by A × B = |A||B|sin(θ)n, where n is a unit vector perpendicular to the plane of A and B.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Vectors:**
 
 
• In **mechanics**, vectors are used to describe forces, velocities, and accelerations.
 
• In **electromagnetism**, vectors represent electric and magnetic fields.
 
• In **computer graphics**, vectors are used to model object positions and transformations.
 
• In **navigation**, vectors describe directions and distances.
 
 
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• **Displacement:** A vector quantity that describes the shortest distance between two points in a specified direction.
 
• **Force:** A vector quantity defined as mass times acceleration, often represented as F = ma.
 
• **Graphical Representation:** Vectors are commonly represented in graphs and diagrams to visualize their magnitude and direction.

questions.question: Momentum of an object is defined as the product of its mass and velocity, hence what are its SI units?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**kg m s–¹**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Momentum** is a fundamental concept in physics, defined as the quantity of motion an object possesses. It is mathematically expressed as the product of an object's **mass** and its **velocity** (**p = m × v**).
 
• To determine the **SI unit** of momentum, we analyze the basic units of the physical quantities involved. The **SI unit** for **mass** is the **kilogram (kg)**, and the **SI unit** for **velocity** is **meters per second (m/s or m s–¹)**.
 
• By multiplying these base units (**kg** and **m s–¹**), we derive the **SI unit** for momentum as **kg m s–¹**. *Hence, option D is correct.*
 
• **Momentum** is a **vector quantity**, meaning it possesses both **magnitude** and **direction**. The direction of the momentum vector is always the same as the direction of the **velocity** of the object.
 
• The unit **kg m s–²** represents the **Newton (N)**, which is the **SI unit** of **Force**, not momentum. *Hence, statement/option B is incorrect.*
 
• The unit **g m s–¹** is a metric unit but not the standard **International System of Units (SI)** unit, as the **SI** system requires mass to be in **kilograms**. *Hence, statement/option A is incorrect.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Newton's Second Law of Motion:** This law states that the **force** applied to an object is equal to the rate of change of its **momentum** (**F = dp/dt**). This establishes a direct relationship between **force**, **mass**, and **acceleration**.
 
• **Law of Conservation of Momentum:** In the absence of an external **force**, the total **momentum** of a closed system remains **constant**. This principle is vital in analyzing **collisions** and **explosions**, where the initial momentum equals the final momentum.
 
• **Impulse:** **Impulse** is defined as the change in **momentum** of an object when a **force** acts upon it for an interval of **time**. The **SI unit** for impulse is the **Newton-second (N s)**, which is dimensionally equivalent to **kg m s–¹**.
 
• **Factors Affecting Momentum:**
 
 
• **Mass:** If two objects travel at the same **velocity**, the one with the higher **mass** will have greater **momentum**. For example, a **truck** has more momentum than a **bicycle** moving at the same speed.
 
• **Velocity:** If two objects have the same **mass**, the one with the higher **velocity** will have more **momentum**. A **bullet**, despite its small **mass**, has immense **momentum** due to its extremely high **velocity**.
 
 
 
• **Applications:** The concept of **momentum** is used in designing **safety features** in vehicles, such as **airbags** and **crumple zones**, which aim to increase the **time** over which the **momentum** changes during a crash, thereby reducing the **impact force**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **CGS unit** of **momentum** is **g cm s–¹** (gram-centimeter per second).
 
• In **Relativistic Mechanics**, the formula for **momentum** changes as the **velocity** approaches the **speed of light (c)**, incorporating the **Lorentz factor**.
 
• The **dimensions** of **momentum** are **[M L T–¹]**.
 
• An object at rest has a **velocity** of **zero**, and therefore its **momentum** is also **zero**, regardless of its **mass**.

questions.question: _______ is measured using the unit "quintal".
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Weight**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Weight** (often used synonymously with **mass** in commercial contexts) is measured using the unit **quintal**. A **quintal** is a historical unit of mass in many countries which is usually defined as **100 base units** of either pounds or kilograms. ***Hence, statement C is correct.***
 
• In the **metric system**, specifically in countries like **India**, **France**, and **Albania**, one **quintal** is exactly equal to **100 kilograms (kg)**. It is a widely used unit for measuring large quantities of **agricultural produce** such as **wheat**, **rice**, **pulses**, and **sugar**.
 
• **Volume** refers to the amount of **three-dimensional space** an object or substance occupies. It is typically measured in **cubic metres**, **litres**, or **millilitres**, but not in quintals. ***Hence, statement A is incorrect.***
 
• **Length** is a measure of **distance** or the extent of something from end to end. The standard units for length include **metres (m)**, **kilometres (km)**, **centimetres (cm)**, and **miles**. Quintal is not a unit of linear measurement. ***Hence, statement B is incorrect.***
 
• **Temperature** is the physical property that expresses **hotness or coldness**. It is measured using scales like **Celsius (°C)**, **Fahrenheit (°F)**, and **Kelvin (K)**. It has no relation to the unit quintal. ***Hence, statement D is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Metric Quintal:** In the **International System of Units (SI)**, the **kilogram** is the base unit of mass. The **metric quintal** is defined as **100 kg**, while a **metric tonne** is defined as **1,000 kg** (or **10 quintals**).
 
• **Imperial and US Systems:** Historically, the **hundredweight** (cwt) was often referred to as a quintal. In the **United States**, a "short hundredweight" or quintal is **100 pounds (lb)**, whereas in the **United Kingdom** (Imperial system), a "long hundredweight" was **112 pounds**.
 
• **Uses in Agriculture:** In **India**, the **Minimum Support Price (MSP)** for crops is usually announced by the government (via **CACP**) in terms of **rupees per quintal**. This makes it a vital unit for **farmers**, **traders**, and **economists** in the **agricultural sector**.
 
• **Conversion Data:** For scientific and trade accuracy, **1 Quintal = 0.1 Tonne = 100 Kilograms = 1,00,000 Grams**. In the context of **bulk density**, mass in quintals is often compared against volume in cubic metres to determine the storage requirements for **grain silos**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **History:** The term "quintal" originates from the **Arabic** word "**quintar**," which was derived from the **Latin** word "**centenarium**," meaning a **hundred**. It has been a standard unit in **Mediterranean trade** for centuries.
 
• **Weight vs. Mass:** While quintal is a unit of **mass**, in daily **commerce** and **general science** questions, the term **weight** is frequently used to describe the quantity of matter. Technically, weight is the **gravitational force** acting on a mass and is measured in **Newtons (N)**.
 
• **Global Variations:** In **Spain** and **Latin America**, the "quintal macho" or "quintal métrico" is used. For example, in **Argentina**, a quintal is typically **100 kg**, but older traditional variations might still exist in **local markets**.

questions.question: The unit of electric flux is represented by which quantity derived from the product of electric field and surface area?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Newton m² per coulomb**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__** 

__
 
• **Electric Flux** is defined as the total number of **electric field lines** passing through a given **surface area** in a unit of time.
 
• It is a **scalar quantity** that describes the strength and distribution of the electric field over a surface.
 
• The mathematical formula for electric flux is the product of the **electric field** (E) and the **component of the area** (A) perpendicular to the field: Phi_E = E · A · costheta .
 
• The SI unit of the **electric field** is **Newton per coulomb** (N/C).
 
• The SI unit of **surface area** is **square meters** (m²).
 
• By multiplying the units of the electric field and area, the resulting unit of **electric flux** is (Newton/Coulomb) × square meters, which is **Newton m² per coulomb**.
 
• The unit can also be represented as **Newton m² C−¹**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__** 

 
• **Weber**: This is the SI unit of **magnetic flux**, not electric flux. It is equivalent to one Tesla-square meter.
 
• **Tesla**: This is the SI unit of **magnetic field strength** or magnetic flux density.
 
• **Joule**: This is the SI unit of **energy** or **work**, defined as the work done by a force of one Newton over a displacement of one meter.
 
• **Volt-meter**: Since the electric field can also be measured in **Volts per meter** (V/m), electric flux can alternatively be expressed in **Volt-meters** (V × m).
 
• The **dimensional formula** for electric flux is [ML³T−³A−¹].
